title: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
problemStatement:
You are given an integer n representing the number of nodes in an undirected graph. The nodes are labeled from 0 to n - 1.

You are also given a 2D integer array edges, where edges[i] = [a, b] indicates that there is an undirected edge between nodes a and b.

Return the number of connected components in the graph.

examples.explanation: There are two connected components: {0,1,2} and {3,4}.
All nodes are connected in a single component: {0,1,2,3,4}.

solutions.detailedExplanation: This solution uses depth-first search to explore each connected component in the undirected graph. We build an adjacency list where each node stores its neighbors (adding edges in both directions for undirected graph). We maintain a visited array to track which nodes have been explored. The key insight is that each time we start a DFS from an unvisited node, we discover a new connected component. The DFS explores all reachable nodes from the starting point, marking them as visited. After the DFS completes, all nodes in that component are marked, so we won't start another DFS from any of them. We iterate through all nodes, and for each unvisited node, we increment our component counter and run DFS to mark its entire component. The final count represents the total number of connected components.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to add edges in both directions for undirected graph (missing neighbors)
Marking nodes as visited after DFS instead of before/during (causing duplicate counting)
Not checking if node is visited before starting DFS (double counting components)
Incrementing counter inside DFS instead of outside (incorrect count)
Using visited set instead of array (works but less efficient for dense node numbering)
solutions.whyItWorks: DFS naturally explores all nodes reachable from a starting point, which exactly corresponds to a connected component. By tracking visited nodes, we ensure each node is counted exactly once. Starting DFS only from unvisited nodes guarantees we discover each component exactly once. The algorithm systematically partitions all nodes into their respective components through exhaustive exploration.
keyInsights: Each DFS call explores exactly one connected component completely
Visited tracking prevents double-counting nodes in the same component
Starting from unvisited nodes ensures all components are discovered
Undirected edges require bidirectional adjacency list entries
Component count equals the number of DFS initiations needed

solutions.detailedExplanation: This BFS solution counts connected components by exploring the graph level by level. We build an adjacency list for the undirected graph and maintain a visited array. The core BFS function takes a starting node, adds it to a queue, and marks it visited. We then process nodes from the queue: for each node, we examine all its neighbors, marking unvisited ones as visited and adding them to the queue. This continues until the queue is empty, at which point we've discovered all nodes in that component. In the main logic, we iterate through all nodes, and whenever we find an unvisited node, we know we've discovered a new component. We run BFS from that node to mark its entire component, then increment our counter. The key difference from DFS is the exploration strategy: BFS explores neighbors level by level using a queue, while DFS explores as deep as possible using recursion/stack.
commonMistakes: Marking nodes as visited when dequeuing instead of when enqueuing (causes duplicate queue entries)
Forgetting to mark the starting node as visited before beginning BFS (causes immediate re-enqueue)
Not building bidirectional edges for undirected graph (incomplete connectivity)
Incrementing counter inside BFS instead of after BFS completes (incorrect count)
Using JavaScript shift() in tight loop without considering O(n) cost per operation
solutions.whyItWorks: BFS systematically explores all nodes reachable from a starting point by visiting neighbors level by level. This naturally discovers exactly one connected component per invocation. The visited array prevents double-counting: once a node is marked visited, it won't trigger another BFS. By iterating through all nodes and starting BFS only from unvisited nodes, we ensure every component is discovered exactly once. The queue ensures we process nodes in breadth-first order, though the order doesn't affect correctness for component counting.
keyInsights: BFS explores one complete connected component per invocation
Marking nodes visited when enqueuing prevents duplicate queue entries
Component count equals number of BFS initiations from unvisited nodes
BFS and DFS produce same result for component counting, differ only in exploration order

solutions.detailedExplanation: The Union-Find approach provides an elegant solution by modeling the component-merging process. We start with n disjoint sets (each node is its own component). The DSU data structure efficiently tracks which nodes belong to the same set. The find operation (with path compression) locates the representative (root) of a node's set in near-constant amortized time. The union operation attempts to merge two sets: if the nodes already share the same root, they're in the same component and we return false; otherwise, we merge the sets by making one root point to the other (using union by rank to keep trees balanced). Each successful union reduces the component count by exactly one. After processing all edges, the remaining count is our answer. Path compression flattens trees during find by making nodes point directly to their root. Union by rank attaches the smaller tree to the larger one, maintaining balance. These optimizations ensure near-constant amortized time per operation.
commonMistakes: Not implementing path compression in find (resulting in O(n) worst case)
Not implementing union by rank (resulting in unbalanced trees)
Forgetting to decrement count only on successful unions (incorrect count)
Using rank comparison incorrectly (should attach smaller rank to larger rank)
Starting with component count of 0 instead of n (wrong initial state)
Incrementing instead of decrementing on successful union (inverted logic)
solutions.whyItWorks: Union-Find models the incremental building of components. Initially, n isolated nodes means n components. Each edge either connects two separate components (reducing count by 1) or connects nodes within the same component (no change). The find operation with path compression efficiently determines component membership. Union by rank ensures trees stay balanced, preventing degeneration to linked lists. The approach is particularly elegant because it directly models the mathematical relationship: components = n - successful_unions. The optimizations ensure α(n) amortized time per operation, where α is the inverse Ackermann function (effectively constant for practical inputs).
keyInsights: Component count starts at n and decreases by 1 for each successful union
Failed union indicates nodes already in same component (no count change)
Path compression makes future find operations faster by flattening trees
Union by rank prevents worst-case O(n) tree depth by balancing merges
This approach is more space-efficient than DFS/BFS (no adjacency list needed in Solution)
Natural fit for problems requiring incremental connectivity updates
